claims.proposition_evaluated: The City's latest published condition ratings available by 2026-09-03 show that Edmonton's Roads asset class was in poor condition as of the inventory date those ratings describe.
claims.interpretation_notes: Latest published measure: the 2025 Infrastructure State and Condition report (IIS03137, Attachment 1). It was presented to the Infrastructure Committee on February 23, 2026, and its inventory describes assets as of December 31, 2024. I take the publication date from the Infrastructure Committee agenda and disagree with gpt-luna's January 21, 2026. The class is the City's own 'Roads' class in Appendix B (p. 37 as reported). It has three nested sub-classes: Paved Roads (D/F 12.5%), Unpaved Roads (100% not rated) and Curbs (D/F 7.0%). By replacement value (C$10,484,313,206) the class is A/B 70.8%, C 16.2%, D/F 11.2% and not rated 1.7%. So p = 11.2%. Primary ladder: 10% ≤ p < 25%, Partially supported. Alternative ladder: 7.5% ≤ p < 20%, Partially supported. The result is not definition-sensitive on the cutoffs. If the not-rated share is excluded, p = 11.2/98.3 = 11.4%, the same band. p is only 1.2 points above the 10% line. I do not remove Curbs from the class, as the brief forbids it. Curbs are a qualification under the City's own label: Paved Roads alone would stay in the same band, and Curbs alone would fall below 10%. The required alternative on length cannot be computed, because neither reviewer who read the attachment found a D/F share by kilometre or lane-kilometre for the class. City target: none found for the Roads class. A target of fewer than 10% of arterials in D/F appears in the 2019-2022 budget, but I have not shown it is in force, and it covers a narrower set than this class. On that target the Roads class figure would sit just above 10%. Trend (qualification 3): gpt reports the previous report at 11.4% D/F as of 2022-12-31. I report this without drawing a direction from it, because the method and composition may differ between the reports. I keep my round-1 verdict. Two other reviewers reading the primary attachment now support it, where in round 1 I had only a third-party transcription.

claims.proposition_evaluated: At least half of the $100 million council approved for CM-20-0330 came from funding sources that permitted road or alley renewal instead.
claims.interpretation_notes: Three City records identify one funding source for the whole $100.000M: Tax-Supported Debt. They are the adopted profile sheet, the council minutes and the Capital Financial Update to June 30, 2023. That is general municipal capital funding, and no record found says it is restricted. FCS02696 also records the City using debt for backlogged renewal in the same cycle (LRV replacement, High Level Bridge, Hawrelak Park), so this kind of source has funded renewal in practice. No grant is involved, so source 9 does not apply. E = $100.0M, X = 0, U = 0: Supported under the primary cutoff (E ≥ $50.0M) and under the alternative (E ≥ $25.0M). Bylaw 20394 (April 2023) authorized borrowing for this project after council had already made the allocation. It records council's choice and is not an outside restriction on the source. Moving the money after that date would have needed council action. This verdict is about source eligibility. It does not say council would have spent the money on roads, and it does not say a transfer occurred. The amount used in the ladder stays fixed at $100.0M, as the brief sets it. The current approved amount is C$99.570M after the June 2025 transfer (gpt; I have not verified it), and E stays above $50.0M on either total. In round 1 I had Not established because I could not reach the profile sheet. The change is explained in verdict_changes.

I read it through the search index.

claims.proposition_evaluated: The $100 million approved for bike lanes equalled a serious share of the infrastructure renewal shortfall Edmonton itself reports.
claims.interpretation_notes: S is taken from the most recent City figure located for 2023-2026: FCS02696 (June 10, 2025), which states the 2023 to 2026 renewal investment shortfall as approximately $1.52 billion. r = 100 / 1,520 = 0.0658. Primary ladder: 0.05 ≤ r < 0.25, Partially supported. Alternative ladder: 0.03 ≤ r < 0.15, Partially supported. The original 'Renewal Funding Gap' in the adopted budget (Table 6: 3,575.584 - 1,945.673 = C$1,629.911M) gives r = 0.0614, the same classification. The verdict would change only if S fell to $400M or less, or rose above $2.0B. City figures over other periods are reported and not classified: about $1.8B for 2027-2030 in 2025 dollars (FCS02696), about $2.8B for 2027-2030 (CTV lead, June 2026) and $4.7B for 2023-2032 (Capital Investment Outlook, reported by others). I withdraw my round-1 figure of about $1.61B, which I derived from rounded percentages and was therefore a constructed S. I keep my round-1 verdict.

supporting_evidence.finding: FCS02696 states the 2023 to 2026 renewal investment shortfall as approximately $1.52 billion. It also says the approved 2023-2026 capital budget is $9.44 billion, of which $2.06 billion (21.8%) is allocated to the ideal renewal investment. I read it through the search index; the file returned HTTP 403.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Prioritization of Renewal in 2027-2030 Capital Budget (FCS02696)
supporting_evidence.source_publisher: City of Edmonton, Financial and Corporate Services
supporting_evidence.establishes: The latest City-published S for the same four years as the numerator: r = 6.58%.

supporting_evidence.finding: Table 6 of the adopted budget gives C$3,575.584M 'RIMS Ideal Investment' and C$1,945.673M 'Funded RIMS Ideal Investment' for 2023-2026 (54.4% funded). The City calls the difference, about C$1.63B, its 'Renewal Funding Gap'. This is as read by gpt; gpt-luna reports the same total.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Adopted 2023-2026 Capital Budget, Renewal discussion pp. 48-49, Tables 5-6
supporting_evidence.establishes: The original S for the same period, under the City's own heading: r = 6.14%.

challenging_evidence.finding: At either City figure for S ($1.52B or $1.63B), $100M is 6.1-6.6% of the shortfall, far below the 25% line for a serious share.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Prioritization of Renewal in 2027-2030 Capital Budget (FCS02696)
challenging_evidence.establishes: The 'serious share' part of the claim fails. The money is still more than a twentieth of the shortfall.

challenging_evidence.finding: Global News reported a $1.5B capital funding shortfall in the current cycle at the June 10, 2025 fiscal update, and another $1.8B expected next cycle. CBC (June 2025) reported the 2023-26 shortfall as $1.5B.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Edmonton capital funding 2025 fiscal update (Global News)
challenging_evidence.establishes: A lead that agrees with the City's figure. It is not the figure used for the verdict.

limitations: The City describes S as approximately $1.52B. I did not check whether the final adjustment of the cycle in June 2026 published an updated 2023-2026 shortfall. Any S between $400M and $2.0B leaves the verdict unchanged.
No City-published roads-and-alleys renewal shortfall for 2023-2026 was found, so the required alternative cannot be classified. Whether the finding is sensitive to that definition is unknown.
No City benchmark or target for the share of the renewal requirement it funds was found. The City reports about 54% funded, and about 31% for the portion funded from unconstrained sources.
No City unit cost (kilometres or neighbourhoods per dollar) was found, so qualification 3 is not reported.

Qualification 4 depends on which version of the budget is used. $100M is 1.39% of the adopted C$7,192.540M (per gpt) and 1.06% of the C$9.44B approved as of June 2025 (FCS02696). It is 4.56% of the C$2,194.927M total funded renewal in the adopted budget, and 4.85% of the $2.06B ideal-renewal allocation in FCS02696. All are approved nominal amounts, not spending.
Different-period figures are reported unclassified under B2: about $1.8B for 2027-2030 and about $2.8B for 2027-2030 (the latter is a news lead).
unknowns: Whether a later City figure for the 2023-2026 shortfall exists from before 2026-09-03.
what_would_change_my_verdict: A City-published S for 2023-2026 from before 2026-09-03 at $400M or less (Supported), or above $2.0B (Contradicted).
claims.suggested_one_line: The $100 million is about 6.6% of the City's latest reported $1.52 billion renewal shortfall for 2023-2026: a real fraction, not a serious share.
claims.suggested_short_answer: The City reports a 2023-2026 renewal investment shortfall of about $1.52 billion (June 2025). In the adopted budget it was $1.63 billion. The $100 million bike approval is 6.1-6.6% of either figure. That is more than a rounding error but far from a quarter, so it is Partially supported under both sets of cutoffs.
suggested_tldr: Latest City 2023-2026 renewal shortfall: about $1.52B (FCS02696, June 2025).
No City roads-and-alleys shortfall for 2023-2026 was found.
